subject: Vocabulary
description: Root RUPT = break/burst: rupture, disrupt, corrupt, interrupt, bankrupt, abrupt, erupt — meanings, usage, exam angles.

questions.stem: The Latin root RUPT means 'to break' or 'to burst'. Which of the following words does NOT derive from this root?

options.option_text: Rapture (from RAPTUS = seized/carried away, not RUPT)
Rupture (direct: break/burst open) (not this)
Disrupt (dis+rupt = break apart/disturb) (not this)
Corrupt (cor+rupt = thoroughly broken/rotten)

questions.explanation: ROOT RUPT = Latin 'rumpere' = to break or burst. Words from RUPT: RUPTURE (break open), DISRUPT (break apart), CORRUPT (co+rupt = thoroughly broken/morally rotten), INTERRUPT (inter+rupt = break between = stop mid-flow), BANKRUPT (bench broken — from Latin 'banca rotta' where moneylenders' benches were broken when they defaulted), ERUPT (e+rupt = break out), ABRUPT (ab+rupt = broken off = sudden/unexpected). RAPTURE = intense joy/ecstasy — from RAPTUS = 'seized' (Latin 'rapere' = to seize). Related to RAPT (completely absorbed), ENRAPTURE, RAPE, RAPTOR (bird that seizes prey). KEY PAIRS TO REMEMBER: RUPTURE (break) vs RAPTURE (joy). CORRUPT (morally broken) vs CORPOREAL (of the body — from CORPUS). UPSC/SSC ANGLE: 'bankrupt' etymology (broken bench) appears in SSC CGL vocabulary; 'corrupt' connects to anti-corruption laws (Prevention of Corruption Act). PYQ FREQUENCY: RUPT-based words appear in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English vocabulary 1-2× per cycle. MEMORY AID: 'RUPT = RUPEE ka TOOT jana' (breaking of the rupee/value).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly fills the blank: 'The CEO's sudden resignation ______ the company's plans for expansion.' (A) disrupted (B) erupted (C) interrupted (D) corrupted

options.option_text: disrupted (threw the plans into disorder/confusion)
erupted (burst out — used for volcanoes, emotions; plans can't erupt)
interrupted (broke into mid-flow — implies the process was ongoing)
corrupted (morally tainted/rotten — plans don't get corrupted by resignation)

questions.explanation: DISRUPT (dis+rupt) = to break apart, throw into confusion, prevent from continuing normally. A CEO's sudden resignation DISRUPTS plans = breaks apart/upsets the plans. ERUPT (e+rupt) = to burst outward suddenly — used for: volcanoes, anger, applause, skin conditions (rash erupted). Not for plans. INTERRUPT (inter+rupt) = to break into something in progress — 'interrupted the meeting', 'interrupted the speaker'. Implies a TEMPORARY break into a continuing process. CORRUPT (cor+rupt) = to make morally wrong; to contaminate data (corrupted file). Plans aren't 'morally tainted' by resignation. KEY USAGE PATTERNS: DISRUPT: meetings, schedules, markets, services, ecosystems. ERUPT: volcanoes, geysers, conflicts, cheering, violence, diseases (skin). INTERRUPT: conversations, speeches, sleep, signals. CORRUPT: politicians, officials, data/files, values. PYQ FREQUENCY: RUPT-family usage and cloze appear in SSC CGL Tier 1 & 2, IBPS PO, SBI Clerk 1-2× per exam.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The word ABRUPT is most accurately defined as:

options.option_text: Sudden and unexpected, as if broken off (ab+rupt = broken away)
Gradual and predictable (opposite of abrupt) (not this)
Loud and disruptive in speech or action (not this)
Absent or missing from a scheduled event (not this)

questions.explanation: ABRUPT (ab+rupt) = Latin ab = away/off + rumpere = to break → 'broken off' → sudden, unexpected, curt. PRIMARY MEANINGS: (1) Sudden and unexpected: 'abrupt end to the meeting.' (2) Curt and rude in manner: 'his abrupt reply offended her.' ETYMOLOGY: imagine a sentence that just stops mid — like a cliff (cliffs are literally called abrupt in geology — an 'abrupt slope' = suddenly steep). ANTONYMS: gradual, expected, gentle, smooth. RELATED FORMS: abruptly (adv), abruptness (noun). USAGE PRACTICE: (1) 'The soldier's career came to an abrupt end after the injury.' (2) 'She was abrupt with the customer, which led to a complaint.' (3) 'The stream drops abruptly at the waterfall.' CONFUSABLE: ABRUPT vs DISRUPT — abrupt = quality of suddenness; disrupt = action of breaking/interrupting. UPSC ANGLE: 'Abrupt' appears in newspaper editorials describing policy reversals, market crashes ('the market witnessed an abrupt fall'). PYQ FREQUENCY: abrupt meaning and usage in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS PO English 1× per cycle.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A business that is BANKRUPT is one that:

options.option_text: Cannot pay its debts and is legally declared insolvent
Has temporarily paused operations for restructuring
Has been acquired by a competitor through merger
Has been penalised by the government for tax evasion

questions.explanation: BANKRUPT = unable to repay debts; legally declared insolvent. ETYMOLOGY: Italian 'banca rotta' = broken bench — moneylenders in medieval Italy operated from benches (banca); when they couldn't repay, their bench was literally broken as a public declaration of default. LEGAL PROCESS (India): Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016 — provides time-bound resolution (180+90 days). National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) handles corporate insolvency. RELATED TERMS: INSOLVENT = unable to meet financial obligations (synonym). BANKRUPT vs INSOLVENT: technically, insolvency is the state; bankruptcy is the legal process/declaration. USES BEYOND FINANCE: (1) 'Morally bankrupt' = completely lacking moral values. (2) 'Intellectually bankrupt policy' = devoid of good ideas. UPSC ANGLE: IBC 2016 = major economic reform; reduced time for resolution, improved India's 'Doing Business' ranking on 'Resolving Insolvency' metric. PYQ FREQUENCY: bankrupt / IBC in IBPS PO, SBI PO GA and English sections; vocabulary meaning in SSC CGL. EXAM TRAP: option B (paused for restructuring) confuses with 'moratorium' or Chapter 11-style reorganisation — bankruptcy is INSOLVENCY, not restructuring.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word ERUPT most accurately?

options.option_text: Cheers erupted from the crowd when India won the match.
The manager erupted the meeting by speaking loudly.
She erupted the news to her family calmly. (not this)
The bank erupted the payment due to insufficient funds.

questions.explanation: ERUPT (e+rupt) = to burst out suddenly and violently. CORRECT USAGE: 'Cheers erupted' — cheers burst out suddenly — ✓ natural and idiomatic. TRANSITIVE vs INTRANSITIVE: ERUPT is predominantly INTRANSITIVE — the subject does the erupting (a volcano erupts, violence erupts, cheers erupt). It is NOT typically used transitively: 'She erupted the news' → WRONG. CORRECT PATTERNS: (1) 'The volcano erupted.' (2) 'Anger erupted in the crowd.' (3) 'Fighting erupted in the border region.' (4) 'A rash erupted on his arm.' (5) 'Applause erupted.' CONFUSED WITH: DISRUPT (to disturb/break up) — 'The manager DISRUPTED the meeting' (not erupted). IRRUPT = to burst into a place from outside (rare; confused with erupt). RELATED: ERUPTION (noun) — volcanic eruption, eruption of violence; ERUPTIVE (adj). PYQ FREQUENCY: correct usage/sentence identification for erupt/disrupt/interrupt in SSC CGL, IBPS PO Tier-2 English 1× per cycle. EXAM TRAP: option B has 'erupted the meeting' which uses erupt transitively — grammatically and contextually wrong.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The word INCORRUPTIBLE most precisely describes a person who:

options.option_text: Cannot be morally broken — immune to bribery or moral compromise
Is uneducated and unable to understand complex moral issues
Refuses to follow instructions from authority figures
Is inflexible in thinking and resistant to new ideas

questions.explanation: INCORRUPTIBLE = in (not) + cor+rupt+ible = not able to be thoroughly broken/rotten = impossible to corrupt morally or materially. A person of incorruptible character cannot be bribed, tempted, or morally compromised. HISTORICAL USAGE: Maximilien Robespierre (French Revolution) was nicknamed 'The Incorruptible' — known for refusing bribes, though later became a tyrant. DECAY SENSE: Incorruptible also means not subject to physical decay — used in theology ('incorruptible body of saints'). WORD FAMILY: CORRUPT → CORRUPTION → CORRUPTED → INCORRUPT → INCORRUPTIBLE → INCORRUPTIBILITY. RELATED WORDS: INTEGRITY (moral wholeness), PROBITY (having strong moral principles), RECTITUDE (morally correct behaviour). ANTONYM: VENAL (corruptible for money), MERCENARY, BRIBABLE. UPSC ANGLE: Incorruptible officials are central to 'Lokpal' debates. Art 311 of Constitution protects government servants from arbitrary dismissal — part of the framework for civil servant integrity. PYQ FREQUENCY: incorruptible / probity in UPSC Prelims Ethics GS-4 vocabulary, IBPS PO Mains 1× per cycle.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: In legal/financial English, RUPTURE of contract refers to:

options.option_text: A fundamental breach that breaks the contract entirely and entitles the other party to treat it as discharged
A minor violation with no legal consequences for either party (not this) instead however
A mutual agreement to terminate the contract before its scheduled end (not this) instead
An extension of the contract period beyond its original term (not this) instead however

questions.explanation: RUPTURE OF CONTRACT = a total break of the contractual relationship — typically used for REPUDIATORY BREACH (a breach so serious that it goes to the root of the contract). When a party commits a repudiatory breach, the innocent party may: (a) accept the rupture and treat the contract as discharged, claiming damages; OR (b) affirm the contract and insist on performance. CONTRAST: MINOR BREACH = small violation; innocent party can claim damages but contract continues. MUTUAL TERMINATION = consensual, no breach. EXTENSION = modification, not rupture. KEY LEGAL TERMS for contract ending: (1) DISCHARGE (completion of obligations). (2) RESCISSION (cancelled ab initio — from the beginning). (3) REPUDIATION (refusing to fulfil). (4) FRUSTRATION (impossible due to unforeseen events). UPSC ANGLE: Indian Contract Act 1872 (especially Section 39 — repudiation by anticipatory breach) and Section 55 (time as essence of contract) are relevant contexts where contract 'rupture' concepts apply. PYQ FREQUENCY: contract law vocabulary in CLAT, RBI Grade B, SEBI Grade A English sections.
